newsitem.title: FRANCE: Versolato plays it safe for Lanvin.
newsitem.headline: Versolato plays it safe for Lanvin.

text.p: - Stewardesses' trouser suits, chiffon cocktail numbers spattered with bright lace, and a pink silk Jackie Kennedy -- Ocimar Versolato played it safe with his summer styles for Lanvin.
The ailing fashion house has gambled on Versolato helping it return to profitability, but his second ready-to-wear collection for Lanvin on Saturday night failed to dazzle the fashion crowd.
Versolato kept Lanvin's matronly clientele in mind, showing black viscose knits for cocktails and scarf dresses with pert little pastel coats.

An occasional spark flew, especially from the draped evening sheaths that are his forte -- some with beaded straps in shades of purple or royal blue, sleek black satin columns, and a jacket of pleated pink faille that spilled over a strapless pearl grey bustier gown.

Jean-Paul Gaultier scored a hit with all-in-one trompe l'oeil three piece suits (neckties included) that models took off with a simple slide of a zipper, string bikinis peeking out from low-cut dress backs and and tatoo bodystockings.

The layering was all topsy turvy, in stride with Gaultier's witty take on reversing the most basic rules of dress -- fishnet stockings over bright green knee-socks, bikini bottoms over denim shorts, sari silk skirts wrapped over trousers and bras on the outside of dresses.
Surely the slacks and long skirts with waistlines dipping low in back to put G-stringed buttocks on view won't make it to the high street.
But it's not Gaultier's crowd-pleasing, far out catwalk shows that make him one of France's leading fashion designers.

So in the midst of the madness were beautifully cut pinstriped suits with knee pants or wide-legged fluid trousers -- someties edged with Indian motifs -- snappy sailor jumpsuits, liquid halter dresses and perfect little shantung jackets.
And for an eyebrow raising finale, the bride, all virginal white from the front, wore a backless dress with a bouquet of lilies on her bottom in place of a G-string.

"I think it was sensational. I loved the suiting, I loved the new prints and the mixes," said Nicole Fischelis of Sak Fifth Avenue department store. "I loved all the cross culture influences, the jumpsuits and sailor items."

Herve Leger's familiar bandage dress made its bi-annual outing -- long, with bound busts over slim crepe skirts in white, sky blue or bordeaux, or in two pieces with skimpy bandage brassieres leaving bellies bare.
They also came as brightly striped tubes in mostly yellow, orange and Chinese red and for evening, in black with chiffon handkerchief skirts.

Otherwise, it was a shortwinded collection offering black and white jacquard knits, zebra stripe jersey sheaths and crepe trouser ensembles in rust or electric yellow-orange with elastic smocking around the torso.
